what: Vail Resorts operates ski mountains. It owns or operates dozens of ski areas in the United States, Canada, Australia and Switzerland, including Vail, Whistler Blackcomb, Park City and Breckenridge, and sells the Epic Pass — a season ticket covering all of them.
customers: Skiers and snowboarders, predominantly North American, who buy season passes in advance or lift tickets on the day, plus lodging, ski school, equipment rental and dining customers at the resorts.
money: Lift tickets and season passes, ski school, equipment rental and on-mountain dining.
Hotels, condominium management and related services at and near the resorts.
moat: A developed ski mountain is irreplaceable: the terrain, the lifts, the permits and the surrounding property cannot be recreated, and no meaningful new ski area has been built in North America in decades. The Epic Pass is the strategic achievement — it converts weather-dependent daily ticket revenue into money collected before the season starts, regardless of snowfall.
risks: Fourteen analysts average a $148.36 target, below the current price of $152.06 — an unusual signal that the sell side sees the shares as fully valued.
Revenue declined from $3.0B in 2025 to $2.8B in 2026, and skier visits have been weakening.
Debt of $3.4B against $268.5M of cash is heavy, and much of it financed the resort acquisitions.
Season pass price increases have met visible customer resistance, and the strategy of raising prices on a shrinking visitor base has a limit.
Warming winters are a genuine structural risk: lower-altitude resorts have shorter, less reliable seasons, and snowmaking has limits and costs.
opportunities: Ski mountains cannot be replicated, and no significant new resort has opened in North America in decades.
The Epic Pass collects a large share of revenue before the season begins, which removes most of the weather risk from a single year.
The shares trade at about 11.8 times EV/EBITDA and 21.9 times free cash flow.
Free cash flow of $248.0M supports a substantial dividend, and the asset base is genuinely scarce.
Pass holders ski more often and spend more on food, lessons and rentals than day-ticket buyers.
watch: Season pass unit sales, separately from pass price. Revenue can rise on price while the customer base shrinks, and the unit number is what tells you whether the franchise is growing.
view: The Epic Pass was one of the best strategic ideas in the leisure industry. Ski resorts historically lived or died on snowfall: a bad winter meant empty slopes and no revenue. By selling an annual pass covering every mountain it owns, at a price that makes it irrational to buy day tickets, Vail moved the money to before the season starts. Pass holders pay in the spring and ski whenever they ski. That converted a weather lottery into something close to a subscription, and the market rewarded it accordingly.

The strategy has reached its limit, and the numbers show it. Revenue fell from $3.0 billion to $2.8 billion, skier visits have been weakening, and pass price increases have met real customer resistance — crowded mountains, long lift queues and resentment among exactly the committed skiers the pass was designed to capture. Raising prices on a shrinking base works for a while and then stops working. Fourteen analysts with an average target below the share price is the market saying it has stopped.

The assets remain genuinely irreplaceable, and this is the floor under the investment. Nobody has built a significant new ski area in North America in decades: the terrain, water rights, permits and surrounding real estate cannot be assembled. That scarcity means the mountains are worth a great deal regardless of how well they are currently being run, and at 11.8 times EV/EBITDA you are not paying much above that asset value.

The risk I weigh most heavily is climate, because it is directional rather than cyclical. Warmer winters shorten seasons and make them less reliable, and the effect is worst at lower-altitude resorts — which is a significant part of the portfolio Vail assembled to feed the pass. Snowmaking helps, costs money, and needs cold nights to work at all. Combined with $3.4 billion of debt, that makes this a scarce asset facing a slow structural problem at a price that assumes neither gets much worse. Pass units rather than pass revenue is the number that reveals which way it is going.
bull: Irreplaceable mountains and a pass model that collects revenue before the snow falls support pricing power, and 11.8 times EV/EBITDA understates the asset value.
bear: Pass price resistance meets falling skier visits, warming winters shorten seasons at lower-altitude resorts, and $3.4 billion of debt sits on a declining revenue line.
